abolish.current_note: its stem 'aboliss-' gave the English form
the abolition of slavery made the word central in the 1800s

absolute.current_note: loosened, unrestricted, from ab- (away) and solvere (to loosen)
settled as the English word for something complete and unrestricted

absurd.current_note: 'ab-', off, plus 'surdus', deaf or muffled: a jarring sound
French 'absurde' is attested in the 1500s; Latin 'absurdus' first meant 'out of tune, discordant'
the 'Theatre of the Absurd' dates from the 1960s

accede.current_note: to approach, to agree to, from ad- (to) and cedere (to go, yield)
settled as the English word for agreeing to a demand or request

accent.current_note: to sing, giving rise to cantus (a song, a tone)
a tone added to speech, from ad- (to) and cantus (song)
carried into French for a distinctive way of pronouncing words
settled as the English word for a distinctive way of pronouncing speech

accessory.current_note: additional, supplementary, from accedere (to approach, to be added to)
settled as the English word for a supplementary item, or one who aids a crime

acclaim.current_note: to shout approval toward someone, from ad- (toward) and clamare (to shout)
settled as the English word for praising someone publicly and enthusiastically

accord.current_note: to bring hearts together, to agree, from ad- and cor
carried into French for reaching agreement between parties
settled as the English word for a formal agreement, or harmony between parties

accordion.current_note: to bring into agreement, from ad- (to) and cor (heart)
German musicians took the term from French 'accord', harmony
coined by Cyrill Demian for the newly invented bellows instrument built around chords
Cyrill Demian patented the 'Accordion' in Vienna in 1829, named for its ability to play whole chords

account.current_note: 'com-' plus 'putare', to reckon, the root of 'compute'

achiote.current_note: named the reddish seeds of the annatto shrub used as dye and seasoning
the Aztecs used the seeds to colour food and body paint, and Spanish kept the Nahuatl name
borrowed into English through accounts of Mesoamerican cooking and dyeing

acquittal.current_note: to satisfy a debt, to set free, from ad- (to) and quietus (at rest)
carried into French legal vocabulary for discharging an obligation or clearing a charge
settled as the English word for a formal clearing of a criminal charge

ad hoc.current_note: literally for this, for this specific purpose
Latin 'for this', used in law and diplomacy for a committee formed for a single purpose

ad infinitum.current_note: to infinity, from ad (to) and infinitus (unbounded, endless)
a phrase from scholastic logic, used for chains of reasoning that never end

ad nauseam.current_note: to the point of nausea, from ad (to) and nausea (seasickness)
literally 'to the point of seasickness', from Latin 'nausea', itself from Greek 'naus', ship

adinkra.current_note: named after Gyaman King Nana Kwadwo Agyemang Adinkra; the Twi root also carries the sense of "farewell", tied to the symbols' funerary origins
the symbols were stamped on cloth worn at Asante funerals; one legend links the name to King Adinkra of Gyaman, defeated by the Asante in 1818

adjust.current_note: the source of Old French 'ajoster', to join, later confused with 'just'
a doublet of 'juxtapose', from Latin 'juxta', near
the spelling was remodelled on 'just', fair

administer.current_note: used for administering the sacraments as well as justice

adorn.current_note: to equip, to embellish, combined with ad- (to)
to equip fully, to decorate, from ad- and ornare
carried into French for decorating something to make it more beautiful
settled as the English word for decorating something to make it more attractive

adult.current_note: past participle of 'adolescere', to grow up, the root of 'adolescent'
'adult' as a euphemism for sexual content dates from the 1950s

advance.current_note: Late Latin, from 'ab', from, plus 'ante', before
the 'd' was inserted in English by mistaken analogy with 'ad-' words

advent.current_note: an arrival, a coming, from ad- (to) and venire (to come)
settled as the English word for the arrival of something significant

adventure.current_note: about to happen, from advenire (to arrive)
carried into French for an unexpected or risky undertaking
settled as the English word for an exciting, risky undertaking

advice.current_note: 'ad', to, plus 'visum', seen, from 'videre', to see
modern French still uses 'avis' for opinion
the 'd' was added in the 1400s to look more Latin

advocate.current_note: to call to one's aid, from ad- (to) and vocare (to call)
settled as the English word for one who speaks in support of a cause or person

adzuki.current_note: the native name for the small reddish bean used in sweets
the Japanese name spread with Western interest in Japanese botany and cooking; the 'dz' spelling reflects an older romanization

aegis.current_note: the shield or protective garment of Zeus and Athena in myth
broadened from the mythical shield to any protective backing or sponsorship

affair.current_note: from the phrase 'à faire', to do

affect.current_note: to do something to, to influence, from ad- (to) and facere (to do, make)
settled as the English word for having an influence on someone or something

affection.current_note: from 'afficere', to act upon, the root of 'affect'
any state of mind produced by influence
narrowed to fond love by the 1300s

affidavit.current_note: to pledge one's faith, from ad- (to) and fides (faith)
literally he has declared, adopted as the word for a sworn written statement

affirm.current_note: a legal term for confirming a judgment or treaty

affix.current_note: to fix, to fasten, combined with ad- (to)
to fasten to, from ad- and figere
settled as the English word for attaching something to something else

affluent.current_note: to flow toward, to abound, from ad- (toward) and fluere (to flow)
settled as the English word for having a great abundance of wealth

aficionado.current_note: to inspire affection, from Latin affectio (affection)
settled in Spanish for a devoted enthusiast, especially of bullfighting
first used in English of bullfighting fans; Hemingway's writing on the corrida popularized it

afreet.current_note: meant "to rub with dust" or "roll in dust"
developed into the name for a powerful, dangerous demon mentioned in the Quran and later folklore
entered English through translations of Middle Eastern folklore and the Arabian Nights

agate.current_note: named for a river in Sicily where the banded stone was first found
settled as the English word for the banded quartz gemstone

agbada.current_note: described the flowing, voluminous ceremonial robe worn by men over other garments
entered English fashion writing via Nigerian and wider West African diaspora culture

age.current_note: contracted from older 'aevitas', from 'aevum', eternity, the root of 'eternal'
formed with the suffix -age, as in Vulgar Latin 'aetaticum'
'Stone Age' and 'Bronze Age' were coined in the 1800s

agenda.current_note: neuter plural of the gerundive of 'agere', to do
first religious duties as opposed to beliefs; the meeting-list sense dates from the 1880s

aggrandize.current_note: to make greater, from ad- and grandis
the extra 'g' was added in English to match Latin-style 'ag-' words

aggravate.current_note: to make heavier, to make worse, from ad- and gravare
settled as the English word for making a situation worse, or annoying someone

aggregate.current_note: to bring together into a flock, from ad- (to) and grex (flock)
settled as the English word for a total formed by combining separate parts

aggressive.current_note: to step toward, to approach, from ad- (toward) and gradi (to step)
narrowed to mean approaching with hostile intent

agile.current_note: French 'agile' is attested from the 1300s; English took the noun 'agility' long before the adjective, in the early 1400s

agoraphobia.current_note: an open marketplace or gathering place
coined by psychiatrist Carl Westphal from Greek agora (open space) and phobos (fear)
coined in 1871 by the Berlin psychiatrist Carl Westphal from Greek 'agora', marketplace

agouti.current_note: named the large, rabbit-sized forest rodent
French colonists in the Caribbean and Guiana recorded the rodent under its Tupi-Guarani name
borrowed into English natural history accounts

ahimsa.current_note: meant 'injury, harm', from a root meaning 'to strike'
entered English through the study of Hindu, Buddhist, and Jain philosophy, later popularized by Gandhi

aid.current_note: a frequentative of 'adjuvare', to help, the root of 'adjutant'
also a feudal payment to a lord
'aid' as foreign assistance dates from the 1900s

air.current_note: Greek 'aēr' was the misty air near the ground, as opposed to bright upper 'aithēr'
also meant a person's manner, as in 'an air of mystery'
'air' as a tune came via Italian 'aria' in the 1500s

akvavit.current_note: literally water of life, a term used for distilled spirits
settled in Scandinavian languages for the caraway-flavored distilled spirit

akwaaba.current_note: a Twi greeting extended to arriving visitors
carried into English through Ghanaian tourism, heritage-return campaigns, and diaspora hospitality branding

alabaster.current_note: possibly named for an Egyptian town famous for producing the soft white stone
settled as the English word for the soft, pale, carvable mineral

alarm.current_note: Italian soldiers' cry 'all'arme!', to arms!, gave the word
to arms!, a battle cry warning of attack, from arma
carried into French for a warning call or signal of danger
settled as the English word for a warning of danger, or a sense of fear

album.current_note: a white tablet for public notices in Rome

alchemy.current_note: the medieval science of transforming matter
Latin translators in Toledo, such as Robert of Chester in 1144, brought Arabic works on alchemy to Europe
carried the study of transmutation into French
settled as the English name for the pseudo-science

alcohol.current_note: a fine powder of antimony used as eye makeup
scholars in Spain generalized it to mean any fine distilled essence
narrowed to mean the spirit distilled from wine
settled on its modern chemical sense

alcove.current_note: came to mean a recessed sleeping chamber
adopted for a recessed nook within a larger room
the fashion for bed-alcoves in Parisian houses brought the word into English architecture

alembic.current_note: a distilling apparatus used by Arab alchemists, from Greek ambix (cup)
settled as the English word for the distilling apparatus

alert.current_note: Italian 'erta', a lookout on high ground, from 'erigere', to raise
a military cry to watch out

alfalfa.current_note: literally the best kind of fodder, a nutritious plant grown for livestock
Moorish farmers brought the fodder plant to Spain; English speakers met the word in the Spanish-speaking American West
carried into American English via Spanish-speaking ranchers

algebra.current_note: from the title of al-Khwarizmi's treatise on equations
entered Europe through Latin translations made in Toledo
also kept a folk sense of "bone-setting" for a time
from the title of al-Khwarizmi's treatise 'al-jabr', 'the reunion of broken parts'; English first used it for bone-setting

algorithm.current_note: literally native of Khwarazm, the surname of the mathematician Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi, whose Arabic-language treatises introduced advanced calculation methods to the West
a mangled transliteration of al-Khwarizmi, entering Europe through Latin translations of Arabic mathematical texts made in Spain
carried into French for the Arabic system of calculation, later reshaped to "algorithme" by false association with Greek arithmos (number)
reshaped by association with Greek 'arithmos', number; the name of the Persian mathematician al-Khwarizmi is hidden in it

alias.current_note: English lawyers used it in writs naming people known by other names

alibi.current_note: Latin for 'elsewhere', used as a legal plea in English courts

alidade.current_note: literally "the revolving radius" or pointer of a measuring circle
the sighting rule of the astrolabe, known to Europe through Arabic treatises translated in Spain
entered English as the name for the sighting arm of a surveying instrument

alkali.current_note: literally the ashes, from the plant ashes used to make soap and glass
settled as the chemical term for substances that neutralize acids

alkanet.current_note: "the henna plant," whose name was extended to a related red-dye plant
adopted a diminutive form for the European dye plant alkanet
entered English for the plant whose root yields a red dye and cosmetic stain

allegory.current_note: literally speaking otherwise, from allos (other) and agoreuein (to speak)
settled as the English word for a story with a hidden symbolic meaning

allegro.current_note: literally cheerful, lively, adopted as a musical tempo marking
Italian for 'cheerful, lively'; the tempo sense came from Italian sonata movements

alleviate.current_note: light, not heavy, combined with ad- (to)
to lighten, to make less burdensome, from ad- and levis
settled as the English word for making pain or difficulty less severe

alliance.current_note: to bind to, from ad- (to) and ligare (to bind)
carried into French for a formal bond between parties
settled as the English word for a formal agreement of cooperation

allocate.current_note: 'allow' shares part of its history with this word

allow.current_note: 'ad-' plus 'laudare', to praise; merged with 'allocare', to assign
two Latin verbs collapsed into one French word
the praising sense died out and 'permit' took over

allude.current_note: to play with, to refer to indirectly, from ad- (to) and ludere (to play)
settled as the English word for referring to something indirectly

ally.current_note: to bind to, to connect, from ad- and ligare
carried into French for joining with another for mutual benefit
settled as the English word for a person or group joined with another for mutual benefit

alma mater.current_note: nourishing mother, from almus (nourishing) and mater (mother)
Latin 'nourishing mother', once a title of goddesses such as Ceres and the Virgin Mary; Bologna's university motto calls itself 'alma mater studiorum'

almanac.current_note: possibly referring to climate or a yearly calendar of the stars
Roger Bacon used the word in the 1260s for astronomical tables; its Arabic origin is still debated
settled as the English word for an annual reference book

alphabet.current_note: the first two letters, meaning ox and house; the Greek letters came from this script
joined the first two letters, alpha and beta
used by Christian writers such as Tertullian

altar.current_note: a raised structure for sacrifice or offering, from altus (high)
settled as the English word for a raised structure used in religious ritual

alter ego.current_note: other self, from alter (other) and ego (I, self)
Cicero used it for a trusted friend, 'a second self'

alter.current_note: reached English in the late 1300s; the sense 'to become different' only appears in the 1580s

alto.current_note: literally high, describing the higher of the low vocal ranges
Italian 'high', because it was originally the male voice above the tenor

alumnus.current_note: from 'alere', to nourish; the same root as 'alimony' and 'alma mater'
American colleges popularized it for graduates

amalgam.current_note: a softening ointment, used in alchemical texts for metal mixtures
carried into European alchemical vocabulary for mercury-metal mixtures
settled as the word for any blended mixture

amandla.current_note: an everyday word for strength, shared with Xhosa amandla
used in the call-and-response 'Amandla! Awethu!', 'Power! It is ours!', at anti-apartheid rallies

amateur.current_note: to love, giving rise to amator (lover)
a lover, one devoted to something, from amare
carried into French for someone who pursues an activity for love, not pay
from the French for 'lover'; Victorian sport made the amateur, who competed unpaid, a social ideal

amber.current_note: originally referring to ambergris, a whale-derived substance
the meaning shifted to include fossilized tree resin
settled to mean the golden fossilized resin

ambition.current_note: literally a going around, describing candidates canvassing for votes
broadened from seeking office to a strong desire for success or achievement

amble.current_note: carried into French for walking at an easy, leisurely pace
settled as the English word for walking at a relaxed, unhurried pace

ambrosia.current_note: literally immortal, the mythical food of the Greek gods
broadened from the divine food to anything exceptionally delicious

ambulance.current_note: walking hospital, a mobile field hospital that followed troops, from ambulant (walking, from ambulare)
shortened and settled as the English word for a vehicle that transports the sick or injured

amen.current_note: the Septuagint translators kept the Hebrew word untranslated
used at the end of prayers in the Old English church, then as a general word of assent

amethyst.current_note: literally not drunken, from the belief the purple stone warded off intoxication
settled as the English word for the purple quartz gemstone

amiable.current_note: carried into French for someone pleasant and friendly
settled as the English word for someone friendly and pleasant in manner

amicable.current_note: to love, giving rise to amicus (friend)
settled as the English word for something done in a friendly, cooperative way

ammonia.current_note: name of the ram-headed god whose desert oracle-temple gave salt deposits nearby his name
Greeks renamed the god Ammon and the salts mined near his Libyan temple after him
coined in scientific Latin by chemist Torbern Bergman for the pungent gas from sal ammoniac

ammunition.current_note: later narrowed to bullets and shells

amnesia.current_note: literally forgetfulness, from a- (without) and mnasthai (to remember)
from Greek 'a-', not, plus 'mnēsis', memory; revived by 18th-century medical writers

amnesty.current_note: literally forgetfulness, from a- (without) and mnasthai (to remember)
settled as the English word for an official pardon for past offenses

amok.current_note: describing a state of murderous frenzy
Portuguese and later British accounts of Malay warriors running frenzied through crowds made 'run amok' a set phrase

amortize.current_note: death, combined with ad- (to) to form a verb meaning to deaden or kill off
settled as the English word for gradually paying off a debt over time

amount.current_note: 'amonter' also meant to climb a mountain, from 'a mont', uphill
the noun 'amount', a total, dates from the 1700s

amphibian.current_note: literally having a double life, from amphi (both) and bios (life)

amputate.current_note: to cut around, to prune, from am- (around) and putare (to trim)
settled as the medical word for surgically removing a limb

amrita.current_note: adopted in English writing on Hindu mythology and philosophy

amuse.current_note: a Gallo-Roman word possibly from 'musum', muzzle, like a dog sniffing with its nose in the air
meant to hold someone's attention in order to deceive them

anansi.current_note: the Twi word simply means "spider", first recorded around 1700-1710 as the name of the trickster figure
carried to the Caribbean with enslaved Akan people and kept as the name of the spider trickster in Jamaican and wider English folklore

anarchy.current_note: settled as the word for a society without government

anatomy.current_note: literally a cutting-up, from dissecting bodies to study them
adopted for the scientific study of bodily structure

ancestor.current_note: Old French contracted the Latin form

andante.current_note: literally walking, from andare (to go), describing a moderate walking pace
Italian 'walking', the present participle of 'andare', to go

anecdote.current_note: literally unpublished things, from an- (not) and ekdotos (published)
broadened from secret historical accounts to any short, entertaining story

anemia.current_note: the same Greek root 'haima' (blood) gave English a whole family of blood-disorder terms ending in '-emia', like leukemia and septicemia

anesthesia.current_note: literally without sensation, from an- (without) and aisthesis (sensation)
adopted once surgical pain relief made the condition medically useful

aneurysm.current_note: a widening, a dilation, from ana- (up) and eurys (wide)
settled as the medical word for an abnormal bulge in a blood vessel wall

angel.current_note: Latin Christianity used it to translate Hebrew 'malakh', messenger
brought by Augustine's mission of 597 and replacing the native word for messenger

anger.current_note: narrowed from general distress to specifically strong displeasure

angle.current_note: 'angle' as a point of view dates from the 1800s

angst.current_note: Kierkegaard's writings on dread were translated with German 'Angst', and Freud's work spread it further

anguish.current_note: from 'angustus', narrow, related to 'angere', to choke, the root of 'anger' and 'anxious'
a feeling of being squeezed by pain
used of both body and mind

anime.current_note: the general term for the art of moving drawings
re-borrowed into English with a narrower meaning

anna.current_note: became the name of a small coin, one-sixteenth of a rupee
British India adopted the term for the currency subunit

annex.current_note: to bind, to tie, combined with ad- (to)
to bind to, to attach, from ad- and nectere
carried into French for attaching territory or property to a larger whole
settled as the English word for adding territory to a larger political unit

annoy.current_note: from the phrase 'mihi in odio est', it is hateful to me
modern French 'ennui', boredom, comes from the same word

annual.current_note: settled as the English word for something occurring once a year

anoint.current_note: 'in-' plus 'unguere', to smear, the root of 'ointment'
past participle used as an English verb

anonymous.current_note: 'Anonymous' as a signature dates from the 1600s

anorak.current_note: British 'anorak' for an obsessive hobbyist comes from trainspotters' typical jacket

antagonist.current_note: an opponent, a rival, from anti- (against) and agonistes (combatant)
settled as the English word for a character or force opposing the main character

antecedent.current_note: to go before, from ante- (before) and cedere (to go)
going before, present participle of antecedere
settled as the English word for something that came before or precedes another

antenna.current_note: the yard of a ship's sail

anthem.current_note: a church chant sung by two choirs alternately
'national anthem' dates from the 1700s, after 'God Save the King'

anthropology.current_note: a human being, combined with logos (study)
settled as the English word for the study of humankind

antibiotic.current_note: against life, describing a substance that destroys harmful microorganisms
coined once penicillin and similar drugs made the concept medically real

anticipate.current_note: to take beforehand, from ante- (before) and capere (to take)
settled as the English word for expecting or looking forward to something

antidote.current_note: literally given against, a remedy given to counter poison
settled as the word for a poison's counter-remedy

antipasto.current_note: literally before the meal, from ante (before) and pasto (food)
Italian 'before the meal', from 'anti', before, plus 'pasto', meal

antique.current_note: Renaissance collectors used it for Greek and Roman remains

antiseptic.current_note: against putrefaction, from sepein (to make rotten)
settled as the medical word for a substance preventing infection

antithesis.current_note: a placing against, from anti- (against) and tithenai (to place)
settled as the English word for the direct opposite of something

anxiety.current_note: troubled, uneasy, from angere (to choke, to torment)
settled as the English word for a feeling of worry or unease

anxious.current_note: from 'angere', to choke, the root of 'anguish' and 'anger'

ao dai.current_note: literally 'long shirt', a fitted tunic worn over trousers that evolved into Vietnam's national dress

apartheid.current_note: literally "separateness", the name of South Africa's system of racial segregation

apathy.current_note: literally without suffering, a Stoic ideal of freedom from passion
narrowed to mean simple lack of interest or feeling

apology.current_note: a speech of defence; Plato's Apology is Socrates' defence at his trial
used for defences of the Christian faith
shifted from a defence to an admission of fault

apostle.current_note: the Twelve disciples sent out by Jesus
later used for any ardent supporter of a cause

apparel.current_note: from 'par', equal: to make things match

apparent.current_note: to appear, to come into sight, from ad- (to) and parere (to appear)
settled as the English word for something clearly visible or evident

appease.current_note: 'appeasement' became a political term in the 1930s

appendix.current_note: to hang upon, from ad- (to) and pendere (to hang)
formed as a noun for something attached or hanging on
settled as the English word for a small pouch attached to the intestine, and later added text

appetite.current_note: to seek toward, to desire, from ad- (toward) and petere (to seek)
settled as the English word for a natural desire, especially for food

applaud.current_note: to clap, to strike the hands together, combined with ad- (toward)
to clap in approval, from ad- and plaudere
settled as the English word for clapping in approval, or expressing strong approval

apply.current_note: to fold toward, to attach, from ad- (toward) and plicare (to fold)
settled as the English word for putting something to use, or making a formal request

approach.current_note: used of troops advancing on a town

approve.current_note: to test, to prove, combined with ad- (to)
to prove thoroughly, to sanction, from ad- and probare
carried into French for officially agreeing to something
settled as the English word for officially agreeing to or thinking well of something

apt.current_note: settled as the English word for something appropriate or likely

aptitude.current_note: settled as the English word for a natural ability or talent for something

aquamarine.current_note: sea water, from aqua (water) and marinus (of the sea)
settled as the English word for the pale blue-green gemstone resembling sea water

aquarium.current_note: first used for a pond or tank for water plants

arabesque.current_note: the people's own name for themselves
coined to describe flowing Moorish and Islamic decorative patterns
later extended to a musical passage (1853) and a ballet pose (1830)

arachnid.current_note: a mortal weaver in myth transformed into the first spider by a jealous goddess

arancini.current_note: an orange, describing the golden, round, fried rice balls' resemblance to the fruit

arbiter.current_note: possibly 'ad-' plus 'baetere', to go: one who goes to see

arbitrary.current_note: used of decisions left to a judge's discretion

arbitration.current_note: to judge, to be a witness, from arbiter (a judge)
settled as the English word for settling a dispute through a neutral judge

arcade.current_note: a plain word for a bow or arch
named an arch, especially of a bridge

arch.current_note: 'arch-' as in 'archbishop' is unrelated, from Greek 'arkhos', chief

archaeology.current_note: settled as the English word for the study of human history through excavation

archer.current_note: English longbowmen won at Agincourt in 1415

archipelago.current_note: literally chief sea, from arkhi (chief) and pelagos (sea), originally naming the Aegean Sea
carried into Italian and broadened to mean any sea studded with islands

architect.current_note: literally chief builder, from arkhi- (chief) and tekton (builder)
settled as the English word for one who designs buildings

area.current_note: an open space in a Roman city

arena.current_note: the sand-covered floor of an amphitheatre soaked up blood

arepa.current_note: a word from an indigenous language of Venezuela for a cornmeal cake

argon.current_note: literally lazy, inactive, describing the gas's chemical unreactivity

argue.current_note: a frequentative of 'arguere', to make clear, prove

aria.current_note: mist, haze, clouds, later broadened to mean the atmosphere or air

aristocracy.current_note: literally rule by the best, from aristos (best) and kratos (power)

aristocrat.current_note: coined during the French Revolution for nobles

arithmetic.current_note: the root word for number itself

armada.current_note: came to mean a fleet of warships

carpenter.current_note: a Gaulish word; the 'carpentarius' built carriages

casual.current_note: to fall, giving rise to casus (a fall, a chance event)

catalpa.current_note: literally 'winged head', describing the tree's showy flower clusters or seed pods

catch.current_note: the Norman form kept the hard 'k' sound

catharsis.current_note: a cleansing, a purification, from kathairein (to purify)

cauldron.current_note: hot, warm, from calere (to be warm)

cause.current_note: both a reason and a case at law

caution.current_note: from 'cavere', to beware; 'caveat' is from the same verb

cavalier.current_note: a horseman, a knight, from cavallo (horse, from caballus)

cavalry.current_note: settled in Italian for soldiers who fought on horseback

center.current_note: Greek, the fixed point of a pair of compasses

chain.current_note: iron chains for prisoners and anchors

chartreuse.current_note: a mountain range and monastery in France where monks produced a distinctive green liqueur

cost.current_note: 'com-' plus 'stare', to stand: the price stands at

cot.current_note: a simple bedstead made of a wooden frame and woven rope

counter.current_note: a table where money was counted

county.current_note: from 'comes', companion, the title of a count

course.current_note: a running, a route, from currere

court.current_note: a king's household and law court

cousin.current_note: literally mother's sister's child, from com- (together) and soror (sister)

covenant.current_note: used for the biblical covenant between God and Israel

coward.current_note: possibly from a frightened animal turning tail, or the hare named 'Coart' in the Reynard tales

crawl.current_note: settled as the standard English word for moving slowly on all fours

credence.current_note: settled as the English word for belief in the truth of something

crust.current_note: the hard outer part of bread

crystal.current_note: literally ice, since clear quartz was once believed to be permanently frozen ice

cube.current_note: a cube, a die used in games of chance

curriculum.current_note: from 'currere', to run; a racecourse or chariot

diameter.current_note: carried into Latin for the line measuring across a circle

dine.current_note: eaten late morning in the Middle Ages

el nino.current_note: literally the child, referring to the Christ child, since the warm ocean current typically appears around Christmas
Peruvian fishermen named the warm current 'the Christ Child' because it arrived around Christmas

elaborate.current_note: past participle of 'elaborare', to work out: 'e-' plus 'labor', work

elate.current_note: to carry out, to lift up, from ex- (out) and ferre (to carry), with irregular past participle elatus
settled as the English word for filling someone with great happiness

elect.current_note: to choose out, from ex- (out) and legere (to choose)
settled as the English word for choosing someone through voting

electric.current_note: amber, which produces static charge when rubbed
coined by scientist William Gilbert from the Greek word for amber
settled as the word for the new phenomenon of electricity

electron.current_note: amber, which produces static electricity when rubbed
coined by physicist George Stoney for the fundamental unit of electric charge

elegant.current_note: from 'eligere', to pick out, the root of 'elect'
Latin 'elegans' was first a term of reproach meaning fussy or fastidious, from 'eligere', to choose carefully
a mathematical proof can also be 'elegant'

elegy.current_note: a mournful poem, from elegos (a song of lament)
settled as the English word for a poem of serious reflection, typically mourning the dead

elephant.current_note: Homer used 'elephas' only for ivory, which Greeks knew before the animal
carried into Latin for the large tusked animal
carried into French for the same animal
settled as the English word for the large tusked mammal

elevate.current_note: light, not heavy, combined with ex- (out)
to lift up, to raise, from ex- and levis
settled as the English word for raising something to a higher position

eligible.current_note: to choose, to read, combined with ex- (out)
to choose out, from ex- and legere
able to be chosen, from eligere
settled as the English word for someone qualified to be chosen for something

elite.current_note: chosen, selected, from elire (to choose, to select)
settled as the English word for a select, superior group

elixir.current_note: a legendary substance alchemists sought to turn base metal into gold
Arabic 'al-iksir', from Greek 'xērion', a drying powder for wounds; alchemists sought an elixir of life
settled as the word for a magical or curative potion

ellipse.current_note: literally a falling short, describing a curve where a cone's slice falls short of a full circle
Greek 'falling short'; Kepler showed in 1609 that planets move in ellipses

eloquent.current_note: to speak out, from e- (out) and loqui (to speak)
settled as the English word for fluent, persuasive speech

elote.current_note: named a tender, fresh ear of corn
Mexican street vendors serve it with mayonnaise, cheese and chilli
borrowed into English food culture as Mexican street corn grew popular

elude.current_note: to escape by trick, to play out, from ex- (out) and ludere (to play)
settled as the English word for escaping or avoiding something skillfully

emancipate.current_note: hand, combined with capere (to take) to form mancipium (formal ownership)
to release from ownership, from ex- (out) and mancipium (ownership)
settled as the English word for freeing someone from legal, social, or political restriction

embark.current_note: a Late Latin word, the root of 'barque' and 'bark'
'embark on' a project dates from the 1600s

embassy.current_note: a Gothic word, borrowed into Medieval Latin as 'ambactia'
the building sense dates from the 1800s

emblem.current_note: from 'emballein', to throw in: an inlaid ornament
a mosaic inlay; Roman villas often had an emblema at the centre of the floor
Renaissance 'emblem books' paired images with moral verses

embolism.current_note: literally a wedge, something thrown in, from en- (in) and ballein (to throw)
settled as the medical word for a blockage in a blood vessel

emerald.current_note: the name for the vivid green precious stone
carried through Latin into French gemstone vocabulary
settled as the English word for the vivid green gemstone

emerge.current_note: to dip, to plunge, combined with ex- (out)
to rise out, to come forth, from ex- and mergere
settled as the English word for coming out from being hidden or submerged

emergency.current_note: to dip, to plunge, giving rise to emergere (to rise out)
a rising up, an unforeseen occurrence, from emergere
settled as the English word for a serious, unexpected situation requiring immediate action

eminent.current_note: 'eminent domain' is a legal term from the 1700s

emir.current_note: literally commander, a title for a Muslim ruler or military leader
the same Arabic word gave 'admiral'; the United Arab Emirates take their name from it

emit.current_note: to send out, from ex- (out) and mittere (to send)
settled as the English word for sending out light, sound, gas, or other matter

emotion.current_note: to move out, to stir up, from ex- (out) and movere (to move)
settled as the English word for a strong feeling stirred within a person

empanada.current_note: to wrap in bread or pastry, from pan (bread)
Spanish 'wrapped in bread'; the Galician empanada is recorded in a 1520 cookbook

empathy.current_note: literally feeling into, from en- (in) and pathos (feeling)
coined by psychologists to translate the German concept of Einfühlung, feeling into another's experience

emphasis.current_note: a showing or appearance, giving special weight to an idea
in Greek rhetoric, a hint implying more than is said

empire.current_note: carried into French for a territory ruled by a supreme authority
settled as the English word for a group of territories under one supreme ruler

empirical.current_note: settled as the word for knowledge based on observation and experience

empress.current_note: from 'imperare', to command, the root of 'emperor'
an emperor's wife or a reigning female ruler
Empress Matilda claimed the English throne in the 1140s

enamel.current_note: Limoges was famous for enamel work

enamored.current_note: to inspire with love, from en- and amour
settled as the English word for being filled with love or strong liking for something

enchant.current_note: to sing a magic spell over, to bewitch, from in- and cantare
carried into French for casting a magic spell, or delighting someone greatly
settled as the English word for delighting someone completely, as if by magic

enchilada.current_note: from 'chile', which Spanish took from Nahuatl 'chilli'
recorded in an 1831 Mexican cookbook, 'El cocinero mexicano'

encore.current_note: literally again, still, used by audiences to demand another performance
French for 'again', though French audiences shout 'bis!'

encourage.current_note: heart, giving rise to Old French corage (spirit, bravery)
to give someone courage, from en- (to make) and corage
settled as the English word for giving someone confidence or support

encyclopedia.current_note: literally a circle of learning, the well-rounded education expected of a free citizen
combined into a single Latin word by Renaissance scholars
settled as the word for a reference work covering all knowledge

endoscopy.current_note: within, inside, combined with skopein (to view)
coined for the medical procedure of viewing inside the body

endure.current_note: hard, giving rise to durare (to last, to harden)
to harden, to make lasting, from in- and durus
carried into French for withstanding hardship over time
settled as the English word for withstanding hardship or lasting over time

enemy.current_note: used for both personal foes and the Devil
largely replaced Old English 'feond', which narrowed to 'fiend'

energy.current_note: Aristotle used 'energeia' for activity or actuality; the physics sense was defined by Thomas Young in 1807
later adopted as the physics term for the capacity to do work

engage.current_note: a Frankish word related to 'wage' and 'wed'

enhance.current_note: the h came from Frankish 'hoh', high

enigma.current_note: the Sphinx's riddle to Oedipus was the classic 'ainigma'; the Nazi 'Enigma' cipher machine took the name
settled as the English word for something puzzling

enjoy.current_note: 'enjoy!' as an interjection is a Yiddish-influenced Americanism

ennui.current_note: from the Latin phrase 'mihi in odio est'

enormous.current_note: 'e-', out of, plus 'norma', rule, the root of 'normal'
'enormity' kept the older sense of wickedness

ensemble.current_note: literally at the same time, together
carried into French for things or people acting together
settled as the word for a group performing or working together

ensue.current_note: to follow after, to pursue, from in- and sequi
carried into French for happening as a result of something
settled as the English word for happening afterward as a result

entertain.current_note: to hold, combined with inter- (among, between)
to hold among, to maintain, from inter- and tenere
carried into French for maintaining or amusing someone through conversation
settled as the English word for providing amusement or enjoyment

enthusiasm.current_note: literally possessed by a god, filled with divine inspiration, from en- (in) and theos (god)
broadened from religious ecstasy to any intense, eager interest

entire.current_note: 'in-', not, plus 'tangere', to touch; also the root of 'integer'

entity.current_note: from 'ens', being, present participle of 'esse', to be
coined by medieval Scholastic philosophers translating Aristotle, who needed a noun for 'being' that classical Latin lacked

entomology.current_note: insect, literally cut into segments, from en- (in) and temnein (to cut)
formed from Greek entomon (insect) and -logie (study of)
Greek 'entomon', cut in pieces, for insects' segmented bodies; 'insect' is a Latin translation of it

entourage.current_note: the sense 'group of attendants' dates from the 1800s

entree.current_note: literally an entry, originally the dish served upon entering a formal meal
settled as the word for a dish served during a meal, later the main course

entrepreneur.current_note: came to mean one who undertakes a business venture
the economist Richard Cantillon used it in the 1730s; Joseph Schumpeter made it central in the 1900s

envelope.current_note: the noun form for a wrapping or covering
adopted for the paper wrapping used for letters

envoy.current_note: past participle, one who is sent

envy.current_note: from 'invidere', to look at askance: 'in', upon, plus 'videre', to see
one of the seven deadly sins

epazote.current_note: named for the pungent-smelling herb (epatl skunk + tzotl sweat/dirt)
Nahuatl 'skunk sweat', from its strong smell; cooks add it to beans to reduce gas
entered English through Mexican cookbooks and Southwestern cuisine

ephemeral.current_note: literally lasting only a day, from epi- (on) and hemera (day)
settled as the English word for something short-lived

epic.current_note: from 'epos', word or song; Homer's Iliad and Odyssey were the models
Virgil's Aeneid took up the Greek form
since the 1980s, casual slang for anything impressive

epicurean.current_note: a Greek philosopher who taught that pleasure, especially simple pleasure, was the highest good
broadened to describe anyone devoted to sensual, especially culinary, pleasure

epidemic.current_note: literally among the people, describing a disease spreading through a population
settled as the word for a disease spreading rapidly through a population

epilogue.current_note: literally words added after, from epi- (upon, after) and logos (speech)
settled as the English word for a concluding section of a literary work

episode.current_note: literally a coming in besides, an added scene in a Greek drama
broadened to any single event, and later a single installment of a story

epitome.current_note: the sense 'perfect example' dates from the 1600s

epoch.current_note: literally a stopping point, a fixed point in time
settled as the word for a distinct period of time or history

equal.current_note: settled as the English word for something the same in size, amount, or value

equation.current_note: equal, even, giving rise to aequare (to make equal)
an equalizing, a making equal, from aequare
settled as the English word for a mathematical statement showing two expressions are equal

equator.current_note: Medieval Latin 'circulus aequator diei et noctis', the circle equalizing day and night
geographers applied it to the Earth

equilibrium.current_note: equal, even, combined with libra (balance, scales)
equal balance, from aequus and libra
from Latin 'aequus', equal, plus 'libra', balance or scales

equinox.current_note: literally equal night, from aequus (equal) and nox (night)
settled as the English word for the day of equal daylight and darkness

equity.current_note: carried into French for fairness and justice
settled as the English word for fairness, or ownership value in property

equivocal.current_note: equal-sounding, ambiguous, from aequus (equal) and vox (voice)
settled as the English word for something open to more than one interpretation

era.current_note: plural of 'aes', copper or brass: the number counted with copper counters, then a fixed date
the Spanish 'era' dating system used 38 BC as its start

erect.current_note: to set up straight, from ex- (out, up) and regere (to guide, direct)
settled as the English word for standing upright, or building something upright

ermine.current_note: the stoat's winter fur was thought to come from Armenia
reserved for royalty and high nobility
judges' and peers' robes are still trimmed with ermine

erode.current_note: 'e-' plus 'rodere', to gnaw, the root of 'rodent'

error.current_note: from 'errare', to wander, the root of 'errant' and 'erratic'
knights-errant wandered in search of adventure

ersatz.current_note: the noun form meaning a substitute or replacement

erupt.current_note: to break out, from ex- (out) and rumpere (to break)
settled as the English word for bursting out suddenly and violently

escape.current_note: literally out of one's cape, describing slipping free and leaving a pursuer holding only the cloak
carried into French for slipping free from capture or danger
settled as the English word for breaking free from confinement or danger

escort.current_note: an armed guard; came into English via French 'escorte'

esophagus.current_note: literally that which carries what is eaten, from oisein (to carry) and phagein (to eat)
settled as the medical word for the tube from throat to stomach

espresso.current_note: literally pressed out, describing coffee forced quickly through fine grounds
Italian 'pressed out'; Achille Gaggia's lever machine of 1947 created the modern crema

essay.current_note: Montaigne titled his reflections 'Essais', attempts, in 1580
'essay' as a verb, to try, survives in formal English

essence.current_note: coined by Cicero from 'esse', to be, to translate Greek 'ousia'
Aristotle's 'ousia', being, was translated by Cicero with 'essentia'

estate.current_note: a standing, a condition, from stare
carried into French for one's condition or property
settled as the English word for a large area of property, or one's assets

esteem.current_note: a monetary valuation before a moral one

estuary.current_note: a tidal marsh or inlet, from aestus (tide)
settled as the English word for the tidal mouth of a river

et al.current_note: and others, from et (and) and alius (other)
short for 'et alii', and others, used in scholarly citation

et cetera.current_note: and the rest, from et (and) and cetera (the remaining things)
Latin 'and the rest'; the ampersand '&' began as a ligature of 'et'

etch.current_note: a causative of 'essen', to eat: literally 'to make something eat', as acid eats metal
Dutch printmakers such as Rembrandt made acid-etched plates a major art form
later used figuratively for something fixed firmly in memory

eternal.current_note: settled as the English word for lasting forever, without beginning or end

ethic.current_note: relating to character or custom, from ethos (character)
settled as the word for moral principles

ethics.current_note: from 'ēthos', custom or character; Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics set the field
used by medieval scholars for moral philosophy
the plural form follows 'physics' and 'politics' for a field of study

ethnic.current_note: the modern sense 'of a people' dates from the 1800s

ethos.current_note: character, custom, the moral character of a person or community
Aristotle's 'Rhetoric' named ethos, the speaker's character, as one of the three means of persuasion

etiquette.current_note: originally a small ticket or label, later the posted rules of court conduct
settled as the English word for the conventional rules of polite behavior

etude.current_note: a word for zeal or application to a task
narrowed in a musical context to a composition meant for practice
popularized in English through Chopin's études, pieces designed to build technique

etymology.current_note: the true sense of a word, from etymos (true, real)
formed from Greek etymon (true sense) and -logia (study of)
carried into French for the study of word origins
settled as the English word for the study of a word's history and origin

euphoria.current_note: literally bearing well, a state of well-being, from eu (well) and pherein (to bear)
a medical term for the feeling of well-being of a healthy person

eureka.current_note: literally I have found it, famously exclaimed by Archimedes upon a sudden discovery
Greek 'I have found it', supposedly cried by Archimedes in his bath; it is California's state motto

event.current_note: to come out, to happen, from ex- (out) and venire (to come)
settled as the English word for something that happens, especially a notable one

evict.current_note: to conquer completely, to recover by legal process, from ex- (out) and vincere (to conquer)
settled as the English word for legally expelling someone from a property

evidence.current_note: literally being seen clearly, from ex- (out) and videre (to see)
settled as the English word for information supporting a claim

evince.current_note: to conquer thoroughly, to prove, from ex- and vincere
settled as the English word for clearly showing or revealing a quality or feeling

evoke.current_note: to call out, to summon forth, from ex- (out) and vocare (to call)
settled as the English word for bringing a feeling or memory to mind

evolve.current_note: to roll, to turn, combined with ex- (out)
to unroll, to unfold, from ex- and volvere
settled as the English word for developing gradually over time

ex post facto.current_note: from after the fact, from ex (from) post (after) and factum (fact, deed)
the US Constitution forbids ex post facto laws

exact.current_note: past participle of 'exigere', weighed out exactly

exceed.current_note: to go beyond, from ex- (out) and cedere (to go)
settled as the English word for going beyond a limit

excel.current_note: Latin 'excellere' meant to rise out above others, related to 'celsus', lofty
the Excel spreadsheet was released in 1985

except.current_note: to take out, from ex- (out) and capere (to take)
settled as the English word for excluding something from a general statement

exception.current_note: to take out, to exclude, from ex- (out) and capere (to take)
a taking out, an objection, from excipere
carried into French for something excluded from a general rule
settled as the English word for something that does not follow the general rule

excite.current_note: Latin 'excitare' meant to call out or summon forth; the emotional sense 'to agitate' dates only from 1821

exclaim.current_note: to shout out, from ex- (out) and clamare (to shout)
settled as the English word for crying out suddenly with strong emotion

exclude.current_note: to close out, to shut out, from ex- (out) and claudere (to close)
settled as the English word for keeping someone or something out

excruciating.current_note: literally to torment from the cross, from ex- (out of) and crux (cross)
settled as the English word for intensely painful suffering

excursion.current_note: a running out, a sortie, from ex- (out) and currere (to run)
settled as the English word for a short journey for pleasure

excuse.current_note: the root of 'cause' is also in 'accuse'
'excuse me' as a polite phrase is from the 1500s

execute.current_note: to follow out, to carry out, from ex- and sequi, with irregular past participle executus
carried into French for carrying out a plan or order
settled as the English word for carrying out a plan, or putting someone to death by law

executive.current_note: formed from execute for a person or branch responsible for carrying out decisions

exhaust.current_note: past participle of 'exhaurire', to draw off water

exhibit.current_note: to have, to hold, combined with ex- (out)
to hold out, to display, from ex- and habere
settled as the English word for displaying something publicly

exist.current_note: to stand, to place, combined with ex- (out)
to stand out, to come into being, from ex- and sistere
settled as the English word for having actual being or reality

exit.current_note: to go out, from ex- (out) and ire (to go)
he or she goes out, a stage direction marking a character's departure
settled as the English word for a way out or the act of leaving

exodus.current_note: literally a way out, from ex (out) and hodos (way)
settled as the word for a mass departure of people

exonerate.current_note: burden, load, combined with ex- (out, away)
to unburden, to free from blame, from ex- and onus
settled as the English word for officially clearing someone of blame

exotic.current_note: the sense 'strikingly unusual' dates from the 1600s

expedition.current_note: literally to free the feet, from ex- (out) and pes (foot), meaning to prepare or set out
settled as the English word for a journey undertaken for a specific purpose

expel.current_note: to drive out, from ex- (out) and pellere (to drive)
settled as the English word for forcing someone or something out

expend.current_note: to weigh, to pay out, combined with ex- (out)
to weigh out, to pay out, from ex- and pendere
settled as the English word for spending money, time, or effort

expense.current_note: to weigh, to pay out, combined with ex- (out)
carried into French for the cost of something
settled as the English word for the cost incurred in doing something

expert.current_note: past participle of 'experiri', to try, the root of 'experience'
the noun, a person with special knowledge, dates from the 1800s

expire.current_note: to breathe out, from ex- (out) and spirare (to breathe)
settled as the English word for coming to an end, or dying

explicate.current_note: to unfold, to explain, from ex- (out) and plicare (to fold)
settled as the English word for explaining something in detail

explicit.current_note: to unfold, to explain, from ex- (out) and plicare (to fold)
settled as the English word for something stated clearly and in detail

explode.current_note: to drive off the stage by clapping or hissing, from ex- and plaudere
settled as the English word originally for rejecting scornfully, later shifting to mean bursting violently

exploit.current_note: the sense 'use unfairly' dates from the 1800s

export.current_note: to carry out, from ex- (out) and portare (to carry)
settled as the English word for sending goods to another country for sale

expose.current_note: to put out, to set forth, from ex- (out) and ponere (to place)
carried into French for putting something on display
settled as the English word for revealing something hidden

express.current_note: to press out, from ex- (out) and premere (to press)
carried into French for squeezing something out or stating clearly
settled as the English word for conveying thoughts or feelings

expunge.current_note: to prick, to pierce, combined with ex- (out)
to prick out, to mark for deletion with dots, from ex- and pungere
settled as the English word for completely erasing or removing something

exquisite.current_note: to search out carefully, from ex- and quaerere, with irregular past participle exquisitus
settled as the English word for something extremely beautiful and carefully made

extend.current_note: to stretch out, from ex- (out) and tendere (to stretch)
settled as the English word for making something longer or larger

extort.current_note: to twist out, to wrench away, from ex- and torquere
settled as the English word for obtaining something through force or threats

extra.current_note: an adverb from 'exter', outside; the same root as 'external' and 'extreme'
probably shortened from 'extraordinary'; later a film extra

extract.current_note: to draw out, from ex- (out) and trahere (to draw)
settled as the English word for removing something, especially with effort

extravagant.current_note: used of papal decrees outside the canon law

extravaganza.current_note: described something wandering beyond normal bounds
a noun coined for extravagant, eccentric behavior
entered for peculiar behavior, then specialized to an elaborate, fantastical stage spectacle

extrovert.current_note: formed for a mind turned outward, toward the external world
Carl Jung introduced 'extraversion' and 'introversion' in his 1921 'Psychological Types'

exuberant.current_note: present participle of 'exuberare', to be fruitful: 'ex-' plus 'uber', udder
first used of lush plant growth

exult.current_note: to jump, to leap, combined with ex- (out)
to leap up for joy, to rejoice, from ex- and salire
settled as the English word for showing great happiness or triumph

fable.current_note: a story, a narrative, from fari (to speak)
narrowed to mean a short story with a moral, often featuring animals

fabricate.current_note: a craftsman, combined with facere (to make)
settled as the English word for constructing something, or inventing a falsehood

fabulous.current_note: the casual sense 'marvellous' dates from the 1600s

facade.current_note: from "faccia" (face), referring to a building's front
adopted for the front face of a building

face.current_note: from 'facere', to make: the made shape

facet.current_note: 'facet' of an issue dates from the 1800s

facile.current_note: came into English through French 'facile'; the sense 'superficial' dates from the 1800s

factory.current_note: a place where things are made, from facere
settled as the English word for a building where goods are manufactured

faculty.current_note: the medieval university's faculties of arts, law and medicine
the teaching staff sense is American, from the 1800s

faint.current_note: 'feint' in fencing is the same word

faith.current_note: Anglo-Norman kept a final 'th'-like sound that Parisian French dropped (modern 'foi'), giving English its ending

fakir.current_note: literally "poor person", from faqura ("he was poor"), describing an ascetic reliant on charity
Arabic 'poor man'; British writers applied it to Hindu yogis performing feats of endurance

falafel.current_note: fried patties made from ground chickpeas or fava beans
often linked to Egyptian 'ta'amiya', made from fava beans, eaten by Coptic Christians during Lent

falcon.current_note: possibly from 'falx', sickle, for its curved talons or wings
the 'l' was restored from Latin in the 1400s

fallacy.current_note: settled as the English word for a mistaken belief based on unsound reasoning

falsetto.current_note: a diminutive of falso (false), a high artificial voice above a singer's natural range

famine.current_note: the Great Famine of 1315–17 struck all northern Europe

fantasy.current_note: an appearance, or the mind's power to form images
carried into French for imagination and whimsical notions
settled as the word for imaginative or unreal ideas

fascinate.current_note: Romans wore phallic 'fascinum' amulets against the evil eye
broadened from casting a magical spell to captivating someone's attention

fascism.current_note: a bundle of rods carried before Roman magistrates as a symbol of authority
literally 'bundle', applied to political associations and unions
coined for Mussolini's authoritarian nationalist movement, consciously invoking Roman imagery
borrowed for the movement and, later, the broader ideology it named

fashion.current_note: a making, a manner of making, from facere
carried into French for the way something is made or styled
settled as the English word for a popular style, or to make something

fastidious.current_note: the sense 'fussy about detail' dates from the 1600s

fatal.current_note: from Latin 'fatum', what has been spoken by the gods
the sense 'causing death' dates from the 1500s

fatigue.current_note: army 'fatigues' were the work clothes for tiring manual duties
carried into French for extreme tiredness
settled as the English word for extreme physical or mental tiredness

fattoush.current_note: crumbs, crushed bread, describing toasted flatbread mixed into a salad
Arabic 'fatt', crumbs, from the toasted flatbread pieces

fatwa.current_note: meant "to instruct by a legal decision"
named a formal ruling given by a mufti
entered English legal and religious vocabulary; gained wide notoriety after the 1989 Rushdie affair

fault.current_note: the 'l' was restored in English spelling in the 1400s and later pronounced

fauna.current_note: a Roman goddess of the earth, animals, and fertility
Linnaeus titled his 1746 catalogue of Swedish animals 'Fauna Suecica', after the Roman goddess Fauna

faux pas.current_note: literally a false step, a misstep

feasible.current_note: capable of being done, from faire (to make, from facere)
settled as the English word for something capable of being done or accomplished

feast.current_note: neuter plural of 'festus', joyful, the same root as 'festival'
a religious festival day; the lost 's' is marked in modern French 'fête' by the circumflex
moved from holy days to the lavish meals that marked them

feature.current_note: a making, a formation, from facere
carried into French for the shape or form of something, especially the face

lyre.current_note: Greek, the stringed instrument of Apollo

sampan.current_note: combining "san" (three) and "ban" (board), describing the boat's flat-bottomed construction

sample.current_note: from 'eximere', to take out, the root of 'example'

samsara.current_note: literally flowing through, the cycle of death and rebirth in Hindu and Buddhist belief

samurai.current_note: literally one who serves, a member of Japan's warrior class

sanctify.current_note: to make holy, from sanctus (holy) and facere (to make)

sanction.current_note: a decree, a binding law, from sancire

sanctuary.current_note: a holy place, from sanctus (holy, sacred)

sang-froid.current_note: literally 'cool blood', a metaphor for emotional composure under pressure

sangria.current_note: blood, describing the drink's deep red color from red wine

sanguine.current_note: a sanguine temper came from an excess of blood, one of the four humours

sapphire.current_note: possibly referring to lapis lazuli, an ancient blue stone; ultimate source disputed

sarcasm.current_note: literally to tear flesh, from sarx (flesh); formed the noun sarkasmos, a sneer or taunt

sari.current_note: referring to a strip of cloth

sarong.current_note: Malay 'sarung', sheath; Dorothy Lamour's 1930s films made it popular in the West

sash.current_note: a fine muslin cloth, often wound as a turban

sashimi.current_note: Japanese 'pierced body', possibly because fish tails were stuck in slices to identify them

sasquatch.current_note: literally 'hairy man', a figure from Coast Salish oral tradition

satay.current_note: skewered, grilled meat served with a peanut sauce

satin.current_note: the Arabic name for the Chinese port city of Quanzhou

satire.current_note: literally a mixed dish, a medley, describing an early poetic form mixing many subjects

satisfaction.current_note: enough, combined with facere (to make, to do)

satisfy.current_note: to make enough, from satis (enough) and facere (to make)

satori.current_note: named the sudden flash of understanding sought in Zen practice

satsuma.current_note: the name of a feudal domain in southern Kyushu that exported citrus and pottery

sauce.current_note: literally salted, from sal (salt), describing a seasoned liquid condiment

saucer.current_note: the cup-plate sense dates from the 1700s; 'flying saucer' from 1947

sauna.current_note: an ancient word for a heated pit-house or bathhouse

sausage.current_note: carried the salted-meat product into French
settled as the English word for the food

savage.current_note: used of cruel ferocity from the 1500s

savanna.current_note: anglicized from Spanish descriptions of New World landscapes

savant.current_note: the verb of tasting, and by extension, discerning wisely

save.current_note: used for spiritual salvation and physical safety

scab.current_note: a skin disease or crust, related to scratching or scraping

scale.current_note: a bowl or drinking cup, later the pan of a weighing balance

scandal.current_note: a snare or trap; in the New Testament a stumbling block

scant.current_note: settled as the English word for barely sufficient in amount

scarce.current_note: from 'excerpere', to pick out, the root of 'excerpt'

scare.current_note: meant to frighten off or avert danger

scarlet.current_note: a fine, rich cloth, later associated with the vivid red dye it was often colored with

scene.current_note: a tent or hut; the wooden building behind the stage where actors changed masks

scent.current_note: the 'c' was added in English in the 1600s, perhaps by analogy with 'ascent'

scheme.current_note: Greek, from 'ekhein', to have or hold

scherzo.current_note: literally a joke, a lively, playful musical movement
Italian 'joke'; Beethoven replaced the minuet with the scherzo in symphonies

schism.current_note: Greek, from 'skhizein', to split, the root of 'schizophrenia'

schmear.current_note: to smear, to spread, related to German schmieren

schmuck.current_note: a vulgar slang term, of disputed further origin

schnitzel.current_note: named a thin, breaded cutlet of meat

school.current_note: originally meaning "leisure", the time available for discussion and learning

schtum.current_note: Yiddish 'shtum', mute; British criminal slang 'keep schtum'

science.current_note: carried into French for organized knowledge

scissors.current_note: from 'caedere', to cut, confused with 'scindere', to split

score.current_note: a notch or tally mark cut to keep count of something

scowl.current_note: related to Danish 'skule', to look down

scrap.current_note: named the leftover trifles or scraps from a meal

scrape.current_note: meant to scrape or erase a surface, reinforcing a similar Old English word

screen.current_note: a panel to shield from heat

scribble.current_note: it may instead be a native English formation from Middle English 'scriben', to write, plus the diminutive '-el'

script.current_note: carried into French for a written document

scripture.current_note: a writing, especially sacred writing, from scribere

sculpt.current_note: related to 'scalpere', to cut, the root of 'scalpel'

seal.current_note: unrelated to the animal 'seal', which is from Old English

search.current_note: meant going round and round looking

seat.current_note: a place to sit, a dwelling

secede.current_note: to withdraw, to go apart, from se- (apart) and cedere (to go)

second.current_note: a second of time is the 'second minute', the second small part of an hour

secondary.current_note: of the second rank, from secundus (second, following)

secret.current_note: to sift, to distinguish, combined with se- (apart)

sect.current_note: a following, a body of followers, a course of action, from sequi

sedentary.current_note: settled as the English word for spending much time seated and inactive

sediment.current_note: a settling, matter that sinks to the bottom, from sedere

seduce.current_note: to lead aside, to lead astray, from se- (apart) and ducere (to lead)

seem.current_note: from Norse 'sœmr', fitting, related to English 'seemly'

segregate.current_note: to separate from the flock, from se- and grex

senate.current_note: a council of elders, from senex (old man)

sencha.current_note: literally 'roasted tea', naming a new method of steaming and rolling green tea leaves

sensei.current_note: Japanese 'born before', a teacher or elder

sentence.current_note: the grammatical sense dates from the 1400s

sentiment.current_note: settled as the English word for a feeling or opinion

sepia.current_note: the cuttlefish, whose dark ink was used to make a rich brown pigment

serene.current_note: 'Serene Highness' was a title of German and Italian princes

serenity.current_note: clear, calm, fair, describing an unclouded sky

sermon.current_note: possibly related to 'serere', to join words

serum.current_note: literally whey, the watery liquid remaining after milk curdles

servant.current_note: carried into French for one who serves another

session.current_note: a sitting, especially of an official body, from sedere

seva.current_note: adopted in English writing on Hindu and Sikh religious practice

shrub.current_note: meaning "a drink", from the same root as "sherbet" and "syrup"

shtick.current_note: literally "a piece", especially a piece of a stage act

sketch.current_note: meaning "a splash" or "a hastily made drawing"

sloop.current_note: possibly from 'sluipen', to glide or sneak

smack.current_note: settled as the English word for a sharp slap or a distinctive taste

solar.current_note: settled as the English word for anything relating to the sun

solder.current_note: solid, whole, giving rise to solidare (to make solid)

solemn.current_note: possibly from 'sollus', whole, plus 'annus', year: yearly rites

solitude.current_note: settled as the English word for the state of being alone

solo.current_note: applied to a piece performed by a single musician

susceptible.current_note: to take up, to undertake, from sub- (under) and capere (to take)

sushi.current_note: originally meaning "sour", describing fermented, preserved fish

suspect.current_note: to look up from below, to mistrust secretly, from sub- (up from below) and specere (to look)
settled as the English word for believing something without proof

sustain.current_note: to hold up, to support, from sub- (up from below) and tenere (to hold)

sutra.current_note: meant 'thread, string', from a root meaning 'to sew'

suture.current_note: a seam, a stitching, from suere (to sew)

swami.current_note: meant 'lord, master, one's own master', from sva- 'self, own'

swastika.current_note: Sanskrit 'well-being'; Schliemann's finds at Troy spread it as a symbol, and the Nazis adopted it in 1920

syllable.current_note: Anglo-French added an extra 'l' to the older 'sillabe'

syllabus.current_note: a misprint of Greek 'sittyba', a label, in an edition of Cicero

syllogism.current_note: literally a reasoning together, from syn (together) and logizesthai (to reason)

symbiosis.current_note: literally living together, from syn (together) and bios (life)

symbol.current_note: 'syn', together, plus 'ballein', to throw: a token broken in two, whose halves were matched to prove identity

sympathy.current_note: 'syn', together, plus 'pathos', feeling; Stoics used it for the cosmic interconnectedness of things

syndrome.current_note: literally a running together, from syn (together) and dromos (running)

syntax.current_note: an arrangement together, from syn- (together) and tassein (to arrange)

synthesis.current_note: a putting together, from syn- (together) and tithenai (to place)

syrup.current_note: a general word for a drink or beverage

system.current_note: to combine, to set together, from syn- and histanai

tabbouleh.current_note: named the seasoned salad now eaten across the Levant

tabby.current_note: a neighborhood of Baghdad known for its striped silk

tabla.current_note: a drum, the root behind a pair of hand drums used in South Asian music

table.current_note: a flat board or writing tablet, the same root as 'tablet' and 'tabulate'

tableau.current_note: a plain word for a flat board or writing tablet

tablet.current_note: medicinal 'tablets' date from the 1500s; computer tablets from the 2000s

tabula rasa.current_note: scraped tablet, from tabula (writing tablet) and rasus (scraped)

tacit.current_note: from 'tacere', to be silent, the root of 'taciturn'

taco.current_note: possibly from a word for a plug or wad, describing a filled, folded tortilla

taekwondo.current_note: Korean 'the way of foot and fist', named in 1955; an Olympic sport since 2000

tahini.current_note: from tahana (to grind), a paste made from ground sesame seeds
Arabic 'ṭaḥīna', ground; the key ingredient of hummus

tai chi.current_note: meaning "supreme ultimate", a concept of balance in Chinese philosophy
Chinese 'supreme ultimate', named after the Taiji of yin-yang philosophy

taiga.current_note: the vast coniferous forest belt of the subarctic, borrowed from a Siberian Turkic language

taiko.current_note: the general word for drum, later specialized for large ensemble performance drums

tailor.current_note: from 'talea', a cutting or twig; the same root gives 'detail' and 'tally'

taiyaki.current_note: literally 'baked sea bream', a fish-shaped cake mimicking a prized fish's form
borrowed as the street snack gained popularity through Japanese dessert shops abroad

take.current_note: replaced Old English 'niman', which survives only in the word 'nimble'
settled as the standard English word for grasping or acquiring something

talc.current_note: the Arabic name for the soft mineral
from Persian 'talk'; the softest mineral on the Mohs scale
settled as the English mineral name

talent.current_note: the Parable of the Talents gave the sense of natural gift

talisman.current_note: from Greek telos ("completion"); meant consecration, religious rite, or payment

carried into French for an object believed to have magical power
settled as the English word for a lucky charm

tamale.current_note: a filled and wrapped cornmeal dough

tamarind.current_note: literally the Indian date, describing the sweet-sour fruit pod

tambourine.current_note: a stringed or percussion instrument, root of several drum names

settled as the English word for the percussion instrument

tandem.current_note: a university pun on 'at length' for horses harnessed one behind another; the two-seat bicycle followed

tandoor.current_note: an ancient word for a clay oven

tangerine.current_note: the port city of Tangier in Morocco, from which the citrus fruit was first exported

tango.current_note: a passionate, dramatic partner dance that emerged in the port neighborhoods of Buenos Aires

tanka.current_note: literally 'short poem', a classical 31-syllable verse form predating haiku

tantalize.current_note: a king condemned to stand in water beneath fruit he could never reach

tantra.current_note: literally 'warp, loom', from a root meaning 'to stretch, weave'

tanuki.current_note: named the raccoon dog, a trickster figure in Japanese folklore

tao.current_note: literally the way or path, the central concept of Taoist philosophy

taoism.current_note: meaning 'the way', the central concept of a philosophy attributed to Laozi

tapas.current_note: literally a lid or cover, since a small snack was once placed atop a drink to keep out flies

tapestry.current_note: the Bayeux Tapestry is actually embroidery

tapioca.current_note: referring to the starchy sediment squeezed from cassava root

tapir.current_note: named the large, long-snouted forest mammal

tarboosh.current_note: adapted the Persian compound for a brimless cap

tariff.current_note: originally meant a notification or definition of terms

tarn.current_note: a small mountain lake or pool

taro.current_note: the name for the starchy root vegetable central to Pacific diets

tarragon.current_note: the Arabic name for the aromatic herb

tassel.current_note: later the ornamental bunch of threads

taste.current_note: first meant to touch or examine by touch

tatami.current_note: Japanese rooms are measured by the number of tatami mats

tattoo.current_note: described the traditional Polynesian practice of skin marking
recorded by Captain James Cook's crew in Tahiti

taupe.current_note: a mole, the burrowing animal whose fur gave its name to a grey-brown color

tavern.current_note: possibly from 'trabs', beam, a structure of planks; also gives 'tabernacle'

tax.current_note: possibly from 'tangere', to touch; also gives 'taxing' in the sense of burdensome

teak.current_note: the name of the durable tropical hardwood tree

technology.current_note: art, skill, craft, combined with logos (study)

teff.current_note: named for its tiny seeds, easily 'lost' during harvesting and threshing

telegram.current_note: far off, combined with gramma (something written)

telegraph.current_note: far off, combined with graphein (to write)
coined by Chappe for his long-distance visual signaling system
Claude Chappe's semaphore towers of 1794 were the first 'télégraphe'

telephone.current_note: coined from Greek roots to name the newly invented device

telescope.current_note: far, distant, combined with skopein (to view)

television.current_note: far, distant, the root of any technology transmitting across distance

tellurium.current_note: the earth, chosen to complement the related element later named for the moon

temper.current_note: possibly from 'tempus', time: the right measure

tempera.current_note: settled in Italian for paint made by mixing pigment with egg or another binder

temperature.current_note: a proper mixture, from temperare (to mix in proportion)
narrowed to mean the degree of heat or cold of a body

tempest.current_note: a season, a period of weather, from tempus (time)

temple.current_note: a consecrated space set apart for religious observance
settled as the English word for a building dedicated to worship

tempo.current_note: applied to the speed of a piece of music

temporary.current_note: lasting only for a time, from tempus (time)

tempura.current_note: meaning "seasoning", possibly linked to Lenten fasting practices of frying fish and vegetables

tenable.current_note: able to be held, from tenere

tenant.current_note: settled as the English word for one who holds property by paying rent

tender.current_note: modern French 'tendre' still means soft and loving

tendon.current_note: the Achilles tendon is named after the Greek hero

tenet.current_note: he or she holds, used for a principle firmly held as true

tennis.current_note: literally hold, receive, called out by a server before striking the ball
settled as the English name for the racquet-and-ball court game

tense.current_note: used by grammarians for verb time

tension.current_note: formed as a noun for the state of being stretched

tent.current_note: carried into French for a portable shelter of stretched fabric

tenure.current_note: settled as the English word for the holding of a position or property

teosinte.current_note: combined 'teotl' (god) and 'cintli' (dried maize), naming the wild ancestor grass of corn

tepee.current_note: meaning "a dwelling", a portable conical tent

teppanyaki.current_note: literally 'iron-plate grilling', coined for food cooked on a flat iron griddle

terminology.current_note: a boundary, an endpoint, the root of a defined term

terra firma.current_note: firm land, from terra (earth, land) and firmus (firm, solid)

terrestrial.current_note: relating to the earth, from terra (earth)

terrine.current_note: earth, the root behind an earthenware cooking dish

terror.current_note: from 'terrere', to frighten, the root of 'terrible'

tertiary.current_note: of the third rank, from tertius (third)

test.current_note: a clay vessel for assaying metals

testis.current_note: literally a witness, applied to the male reproductive gland as a witness to virility

tete-a-tete.current_note: originally an earthenware pot or jug; a humorous Vulgar Latin shift gave it the sense of 'head'

text.current_note: literally something woven, a style of writing, from texere (to weave)

texture.current_note: a weaving, a web, from texere (to weave)

thali.current_note: meant 'earthen dish, vessel', from a word for 'ground, place'

theater.current_note: literally "a place for viewing", from "theasthai" (to behold)

their.current_note: genitive plural of the demonstrative 'sá', 'that one'

theocracy.current_note: settled as the English word for government by religious authority

theology.current_note: formed from Greek theos (god) and -logia (study of)

theorem.current_note: a thing to be looked at or considered, from theorein (to look at)

theory.current_note: in science, a well-tested explanation, not a guess

thermometer.current_note: hot, combined with metron (measure) for an instrument measuring heat
