thermostat.current_note: coined from Greek thermos (hot) and statos (standing) for a device that keeps temperature steady

thesaurus.current_note: Roman writers used it for a treasury or storehouse

thesis.current_note: from 'tithenai', to put; also a term for the downbeat in music

they.current_note: a Norse pronoun that gradually replaced the native English forms hie and hi

thorax.current_note: originally a breastplate, later the chest itself

though.current_note: a conjunction expressing contrast, reinforcing a native English form

thrall.current_note: a slave, a bondsman, someone in servitude

thrift.current_note: prosperity, success, related to thrifask (to thrive)

throne.current_note: a Greek word for a chair of state

thrust.current_note: 'thrust' in engineering, the push of a jet or rocket, dates from the 1800s

thug.current_note: a member of an organized band of robbers and stranglers

tiara.current_note: a tall, peaked headdress worn by Persian kings and nobles

tibia.current_note: the shin bone, also the name for an ancient flute once made from animal shin bones

ticket.current_note: a small note or label attached to something

tidings.current_note: events, happenings, news of what has occurred

tiger.current_note: sharp, pointed / arrow, an Iranian root possibly describing the animal's speed or its spotted look

tight.current_note: described anything closely packed or watertight, such as a well-built ship

tiki.current_note: a carved figure representing an ancestor or deity

tilapia.current_note: a general Setswana word for fish, used across southern Africa

till.current_note: to, until, marking an endpoint in time or space

timbre.current_note: a drum, the root behind the quality distinguishing musical sounds

tiramisu.current_note: literally pick me up, referring to the espresso and cocoa in the layered dessert

tissue.current_note: biological 'tissue' dates from the 1800s; paper tissues from the 1900s

titan.current_note: one of a race of primordial giant deities who ruled before the Olympian gods

title.current_note: used for a label on a book scroll or tomb

toast.current_note: past participle of 'torrere', to parch, the root of 'torrid' and 'torrent'

toboggan.current_note: the name for a sled made of bound wooden strips

toddy.current_note: the fermented or unfermented sap of a palm tree

tofu.current_note: adopted the dish from Chinese cuisine

toilet.current_note: literally a little cloth, originally the cloth covering a dressing table

tokoloshe.current_note: a dwarf-like trickster spirit in Nguni folklore, also borrowed as Zulu utokoloshe

tom yum.current_note: literally boiled and mixed, describing the hot and sour soup's preparation

tomatillo.current_note: the root word for a plump fruit encased in a papery husk

tone.current_note: Greek, from 'teinein', to stretch, like a string

topaz.current_note: possibly named for an island in the Red Sea where a yellow stone was mined

topee.current_note: the everyday word for a hat or cap

topic.current_note: Aristotle's work on 'topoi', commonplaces or stock arguments, from 'topos', place

torah.current_note: literally instruction or teaching, the foundational text of Judaism

torch.current_note: twisted strands of tow soaked in pitch

torii.current_note: named the traditional gateway marking the entrance to a Shinto shrine

tornado.current_note: a thunderstorm, from tronar (to thunder), later applied to violent windstorms

torrent.current_note: boiling, roaring, from torrere (to parch, to burn)

torso.current_note: a ceremonial staff, also used to mean a plant stalk

torture.current_note: carried into French for the deliberate infliction of severe pain

tostones.current_note: settled in the Caribbean for twice-fried, flattened green plantain slices

total.current_note: 'total' as a verb, to wreck a car, is 1950s slang

toucan.current_note: the Tupi name for the large-billed bird

touch.current_note: an imitative Vulgar Latin word, like 'tok' for a knock

tour.current_note: from Greek 'tornos', a tool for drawing circles

tournament.current_note: from tourner (to turn), describing knights wheeling their horses in a mock combat

towel.current_note: a Germanic word related to Old English 'þwean', to wash

visible.current_note: Latin 'visibilis' came from 'videre', to see; the sense 'publicly prominent' is from the 1950s

vision.current_note: settled as the English word for the ability to see, or a mental image of the future

visit.current_note: a frequentative of 'visere', to look at
originally God's 'visitation' of blessing or punishment

vista.current_note: literally a view, a sight, from vedere (to see)
Italian 'view'; landscaped gardens of the 1700s framed vistas

vital.current_note: of life, essential to life, from vita
settled as the English word for something absolutely necessary or full of life

vitality.current_note: settled as the English word for energetic strength and liveliness

vivace.current_note: literally lively, vivacious, from Latin vivax (lively, long-lived)

vivid.current_note: full of life, lively, from vivere
settled as the English word for something producing strong, clear images or colors

vizier.current_note: literally a helper, a high-ranking political advisor to a Muslim ruler
from Arabic 'wazīr', burden-bearer; the Grand Vizier ran the Ottoman government
settled as the English word for a high-ranking Muslim government official

vocabulary.current_note: settled as the English word for the body of words known or used

vocal.current_note: settled as the English word for something relating to the human voice

vocation.current_note: a religious 'calling', the root of 'voice' and 'vocal'
a calling, a summons, from vocare
settled as the English word for a strong feeling of suitability for a particular career

vociferous.current_note: to cry out, to carry the voice, from vox (voice) and ferre (to carry)
settled as the English word for expressing opinions loudly and forcefully

vodka.current_note: the common Slavic root word for water
literally "little water", a diminutive of voda
Russian 'little water'; Russian and Polish records of it date from the 1400s–1500s

vogue.current_note: an Italian verb for sailing along
being carried along by the current of fashion

voice.current_note: Old French 'vois' still pronounced the s
grammar's active and passive 'voice' dates from the 1300s

volcano.current_note: the Roman god of fire and metalworking
named after the fiery Sicilian island associated with the god
named after Vulcano island near Sicily, thought to be the forge of Vulcan

volley.current_note: a noun formed from the past participle of voler, describing flight
entered for the simultaneous discharge of many guns, later extended in sports to striking a ball while it is still airborne

voluble.current_note: settled as the English word for someone talking fluently and rapidly

volume.current_note: to roll, giving rise to volumen (a roll, a scroll)
a roll of writing, a scroll, from volvere
carried into French for a scroll or bound book
settled as the English word for a book, or an amount of space or loudness

voodoo.current_note: meaning "spirit" or "deity", a West African religious tradition
carried to Haiti by enslaved West Africans and blended with Catholic elements
from Fon 'vodun', spirit; Marie Laveau was the famous voodoo queen of New Orleans

voracious.current_note: settled as the English word for an eager, insatiable appetite

vortex.current_note: settled as the word for a whirling mass of fluid or air

vote.current_note: Latin-trained Scottish lawyers and churchmen borrowed it directly from 'votum'
spread into English in the 1500s, keeping the Scottish political sense

voucher.current_note: 'vouch' first meant to call someone into court to prove a title
settled as the English word for a document entitling the holder to a good or service

vow.current_note: from 'vovere', to promise solemnly, the root of 'vote' and 'devote'

vowel.current_note: voice, combined into vocalis (sounding, of the voice)
a letter that sounds by itself, from vox (voice)
carried into French for a sounding letter
settled as the English word for a speech sound made with an open vocal tract

voyage.current_note: provisions for a journey, from via (a road, a way)
carried into French for a journey, especially by sea
settled as the English word for a long journey, especially by sea or in space

voyeur.current_note: Havelock Ellis and other sexologists introduced the word around 1900

vulgar.current_note: Jerome's Latin Bible was called the 'Vulgate', the common version
of the common people, ordinary, from vulgus
settled as the English word originally for something common, later shifting to mean crude

vulture.current_note: possibly from 'vellere', to pluck or tear
'vulture' for a greedy person dates from the 1600s

wadi.current_note: Arabic 'valley'; Wadi Rum in Jordan is famous from 'Lawrence of Arabia'

wafer.current_note: a Frankish word related to 'weave' and to Dutch 'wafel', waffle
a thin cake with a honeycomb pattern

wag.current_note: 'wag', a joker, is a separate word, possibly from 'waghalter', gallows bird
settled as the English word for moving something rapidly side to side

wagon.current_note: the Dutch word for a wheeled cart
Dutch carriers and Low Countries soldiers brought 'wagon' to English

wagyu.current_note: Japanese cattle, referring to breeds prized for heavily marbled meat
Japanese 'Japanese cattle'; Kobe beef is a famous wagyu brand

wahine.current_note: the general word for woman across Polynesian languages
Hawaiian surf culture spread it in 1950s–60s California

wait.current_note: a Frankish word related to 'wake' and 'watch'
'waiter' for a restaurant server dates from the 1600s

walrus.current_note: a compound literally meaning 'horse-whale', naming the tusked Arctic mammal
the Norse compound was folk-etymologically inverted and reshaped under influence of Dutch 'walvis' (whale) and 'ros' (horse)
Dutch 'walrus', from Norse 'hrosshvalr', horse-whale; Lewis Carroll's 'The Walrus and the Carpenter' (1871) made it familiar

waltz.current_note: from "walzen", to roll or turn, describing the dance's turning steps
considered scandalous at first for its close hold between partners

wampum.current_note: shortened by English colonists in New England

wand.current_note: a slender, flexible stick or switch, possibly related to 'wind' in the sense of bending
used for a young shoot and for a rod of authority carried by officials
the magical sense, a rod used by conjurers and fairies, became prominent in Renaissance literature

wanderlust.current_note: German 'wandering desire', associated with Romantic hiking culture

want.current_note: 'want' first meant 'lack', as in 'for want of a nail'
broadened from lacking something to desiring it

wapiti.current_note: literally 'white rump', describing the elk's pale rear patch
Shawnee 'white rump'; the naturalist Benjamin Smith Barton promoted the name in 1806

warden.current_note: a Frankish word, related to 'ward' and 'guard'
Norman French form; Parisian French said 'gardien'

wardrobe.current_note: literally guard robe, from garder (to guard) and robe (garment)
settled as the English word for a room or cabinet for storing clothes

warrant.current_note: a guarantee, a protector, related to guaranteeing something's truth
carried into French for a guarantee or authorization
settled as the English word for an official document authorizing an action

warranty.current_note: to protect, to guard, a Germanic root of the Franks
adapted from Frankish for a formal guarantee of quality or condition
settled as the English word for a written guarantee of a product's quality

wasabi.current_note: a pungent green root used as a condiment, related to horseradish
true wasabi grows in cold mountain streams; most 'wasabi' abroad is dyed horseradish

washi.current_note: literally 'Japanese paper', made by hand from local plant fibers
Japanese 'Japanese paper', made from kōzo mulberry bark; UNESCO listed it in 2014

wat.current_note: a thick, spicy stew central to Ethiopian and Eritrean cuisine
Amharic 'wot', a stew eaten on injera; doro wat, chicken stew, is Ethiopia's national dish

weak.current_note: settled as the standard English word for lacking strength

whirl.current_note: settled as the English word for rapid rotational movement

whiskey.current_note: literally "water of life", describing distilled spirits
the same phrase used for Highland distilled spirits
clipped from the Gaelic phrase and anglicized

wickiup.current_note: meant 'house' or 'dwelling', from the shared Algonquian root 'wik-' meaning 'to dwell'
borrowed into English, first applied to Great Lakes dwellings and later to southwestern brush shelters

wiggle.current_note: a repeated-action form of 'wiegen', to rock, itself from 'wiege' (cradle)
settled into its modern spelling once used as a noun for the motion itself

wigwam.current_note: meaning "their house", a domed dwelling of bent poles and bark
Abenaki 'wikewam', dwelling; the word spread to other Native dwellings

wiki.current_note: adopted for quickly editable collaborative websites

window.current_note: literally wind eye, an opening in a wall for air and light
settled as the English word for a glazed opening in a wall

wing.current_note: the limb a bird uses to fly, replacing the earlier native English word fethra in general use
settled as the standard English word for a bird's or aircraft's flying limb

wiseacre.current_note: reshaped by folk etymology as if from 'acre', and used sarcastically

wok.current_note: the round-bottomed cooking pan used across Chinese cuisine

wombat.current_note: the name for the stocky, burrowing marsupial
from Dharug 'wambad'; wombats produce cube-shaped droppings

wonton.current_note: a small dumpling of meat wrapped in thin dough
Cantonese 'swallowing clouds', a pun on the dumplings' look in broth

woodchuck.current_note: the name for the burrowing rodent, reshaped by folk etymology into "woodchuck"
adopted and reshaped by English colonists in North America

worsted.current_note: a village in Norfolk, England, once a center of fine wool weaving
settled as the word for the smooth, tightly spun wool yarn from the village

wrong.current_note: settled as the word for anything incorrect or unjust

wunderkind.current_note: wonder child, describing a child of extraordinary talent
German 'wonder child', applied to child prodigies like Mozart

wushu.current_note: literally 'martial art', adopted as the official modern term covering Chinese fighting arts and sport forms
borrowed as competitive wushu spread internationally through sport federations

xalam.current_note: blends xala ("to cast a spell") with the onomatopoeic kalam, echoing the instrument's thumping sound
griots accompany songs of praise and history on the xalam

xebec.current_note: originally meant "a net," later "a small warship," perhaps from its fishing-boat origins
adopted for the fast three-masted Mediterranean vessel favored by Barbary corsairs
carried the ship's name into French naval vocabulary
entered English naval terminology for the Mediterranean sailing vessel

xenon.current_note: literally stranger, foreign, describing the rare, unfamiliar gas
coined by its discoverers for the rare inert gas

xenophobia.current_note: Greek 'xenia', hospitality to strangers, was a sacred duty under Zeus
formed from Greek xenos (stranger) and phobos (fear)

xylophone.current_note: the root of 'xylem', a plant's woody tissue
formed from Greek xylon (wood) and phone (sound), for the wooden-barred percussion instrument
Greek 'wood-sound'; Saint-Saëns used it in 'Danse macabre' (1874) to depict rattling bones

yacht.current_note: short for "jachtschip", a fast hunting or pursuit ship
Dutch 'jacht', hunting ship; the Dutch gave Charles II a yacht in 1660, starting English yachting

yak.current_note: the Tibetan name for the long-haired mountain bovine
Tibetan 'gyag', male yak; the Himalayan animal provides milk, wool and transport

yakitori.current_note: literally 'grilled bird', skewered chicken sold at street stalls
borrowed as Japanese-style grill restaurants opened abroad

yakka.current_note: from the Yagara language of the Brisbane area; 'hard yakka' is common Australian slang

yakuza.current_note: named after 8-9-3, the worst possible hand in a card game, symbolizing worthlessness
picked up by English-language journalism covering Japanese organized crime

yam.current_note: literally to eat, describing the starchy root eaten across West Africa
settled as the word for the starchy tuber

yamen.current_note: named the office and residence of a local government official
Chinese 'office of the flags', from the banners outside a magistrate's gate

yankee.current_note: a common Dutch nickname ("John Cheese") mockingly applied to Dutch colonists
the English then turned the nickname on New England colonists

yantra.current_note: from a root meaning 'to restrain, support', denoting an instrument or device
adopted in English writing on Hindu and tantric ritual for a mystical geometric diagram

yashmak.current_note: developed into the name for a face veil covering all but the eyes
entered English through descriptions of Ottoman women's dress

yassa.current_note: described the method of marinating and stewing meat or fish in an onion sauce
entered English through Senegalese restaurants and cookbooks describing the dish

yaupon.current_note: combined a word for 'tree' and 'leaf', naming a caffeinated holly shrub used for tea
Catawba 'yą́pą', little tree; the Timucua and other peoples brewed it as the 'black drink'

yemaya.current_note: compound of iye ("mother"), ọmọ ("child"), and ẹja ("fish"): "mother whose children are like the fish"
creolized in Cuba as enslaved Yoruba carried her worship into Santería/Lucumí practice
spread into English through Santería and wider diaspora spiritual writing

yenta.current_note: originally a woman's given name, later applied to a gossipy, meddlesome woman
a Yiddish woman's name, from Italian 'gentile', later a nickname for a gossip; 'Fiddler on the Roof' made it famous

yerba mate.current_note: herb, combined with Quechua mati (a cup or gourd), naming both the plant and vessel
Spanish 'herb' plus Quechua 'mati', gourd; drunk through a metal straw, the bombilla

yin yang.current_note: representing complementary opposite forces in Chinese philosophy
Chinese 'shade' and 'sun'; the 'Book of Changes' built its philosophy on the pair

yodel.current_note: imitative of the rapid pitch-shifting singing style of the Alps
German 'jodeln', from the syllable 'jo'; Tyrolean singing troupes toured Britain and America in the 1820s–30s

yoga.current_note: Swami Vivekananda's 1893 Chicago lectures introduced yoga to American audiences

yogi.current_note: one who practices yoga, from yoga (union, discipline)
Sanskrit 'one who practises yoga'; Paramahansa Yogananda's 'Autobiography of a Yogi' (1946) popularized it

yogurt.current_note: Turkish 'yoğurt', from 'yoğurmak', to knead; Élie Metchnikoff's 1900s research made it a health food

yuga.current_note: literally 'yoke', extended to mean 'a generation' or 'a cosmic age'
adopted in English writing on Hindu cosmology

yukata.current_note: literally 'bathing cloth', a light cotton robe originally worn after bathing
Japanese 'bathing garment', first worn after bathing at Heian-era hot springs

yurt.current_note: a round, portable felt-covered tent used by nomadic peoples of Central Asia
from a Turkic word for homeland; in Mongolian the tent is called 'ger'

yuzu.current_note: the native name for a fragrant, sour East Asian citrus fruit
thought to originate in the Yangtze region of China; in Japan yuzu baths are taken at the winter solstice

za'atar.current_note: the name for a wild thyme herb, and the spice blend made from it
Arabic for wild thyme; Lebanese man'oushe flatbread is topped with za'atar and olive oil

zany.current_note: the dialect form of the name became the stock bumbling-servant character of commedia dell'arte
entered as a noun for the stock fool character, then as an adjective for clownish, imitative foolishness

zealous.current_note: settled as the English word for showing great energy and enthusiasm

zebra.current_note: Portuguese 'zevra', wild ass, a name first used for an extinct Iberian wild horse
Duarte Lopes's 1591 account of the Congo described the zebra

zeitgeist.current_note: combining "Zeit" with "Geist" (spirit), coined in German philosophy
German 'time spirit'; Hegel's philosophy of history made the idea famous

zen.current_note: Chinese 'chan', from Sanskrit 'dhyāna', meditation; Bodhidharma is its legendary founder
Eisai and Dōgen brought Zen schools from China to Japan around 1200
D. T. Suzuki's English books of the 1920s–50s spread Zen in the West

zenith.current_note: meaning "path" or "direction", from "samt ar-ra's" (path over the head)
a scribe misread Arabic 'samt', path, as 'senit'
settled as the English astronomical term

zephyr.current_note: the god of the gentle west wind
settled as the English word for a soft, gentle breeze

zeppelin.current_note: a surname taken from the village of Zepelin in northern Germany
named for Count Ferdinand von Zeppelin, who perfected the rigid airship's design
shortened and adopted into English for any rigid airship

zero.current_note: the Indian mathematical concept of "void" or emptiness
translated the Sanskrit concept; also the root of "cipher"
introduced to Europe through Fibonacci's writings on Arabic numerals
shortened and adopted directly from Italian

zinc.current_note: named by metallurgist Paracelsus, possibly from Zinke (prong), describing the metal's jagged crystal form
settled as the English name for the bluish-white metallic element

zombie.current_note: referred to a spirit of the dead or a minor deity
took on the folklore meaning of a soulless reanimated corpse
popularized by American travel writing and horror films

zone.current_note: literally "a belt" or "girdle", used for bands of the Earth's surface
adopted for the Earth's climatic bands
settled as the English word for a defined area

zoo.current_note: short for London's 'Zoological Gardens', opened in 1828

zoology.current_note: formed from Greek zoon (animal) and -logia (study of)
settled as the English word for the scientific study of animals

zucchini.current_note: a diminutive of zucca (pumpkin, gourd), a small summer squash
Italian 'little squash'; British English calls it 'courgette', from French

zulu.current_note: the root word from which the Zulu royal clan's founder took his name
his descendants and followers became known as amaZulu, 'the people of Zulu'
from the ancestor Zulu kaMalandela, whose name means 'heaven'; Shaka built the Zulu kingdom in the 1810s
